analysis.one_liner: Lifted the trans-Alaska pipeline's oil-spill liability cap and charged shippers a fee to fund spill cleanup.
analysis.headline: Introduced after the Exxon Valdez spilled 11 million gallons, the bill to lift the pipeline's liability cap and charge oil shippers a 5-cent-per-barrel cleanup fee died in committee without a floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Six months after the Exxon Valdez spill, this bill would have repealed the 1973 law's cap on the trans-Alaska pipeline operator's liability for oil pollution, charged a 5-cent-per-barrel fee on oil moving through the pipeline to fund spill prevention and response, and set a $1,000-per-barrel minimum penalty for discharges anywhere along the pipeline-to-tanker route. It also would have created a citizens' advisory council with a legal right to inspect terminal facilities, a presidential task force to audit the whole pipeline system, and an Alaska oil spill research institute. The bill died in committee without ever reaching the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents of Prince William Sound, commercial fishermen, Alaska Native corporations, and port communities such as Puget Sound, the San Francisco Bay Area, and Los Angeles/Long Beach that receive Alaskan oil; also taxpayers, who were left exposed if the capped liability fund proved too small to cover a multi-billion-dollar spill.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Alaska coastal residents, fishermen, and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Repealed the statutory cap on how much the pipeline's operator must pay for oil pollution damages, and tightened the standard so the company could not escape blame by pointing to another contributing cause.

Imposed a 5-cent-per-barrel fee on oil carried through the pipeline, with the money reserved for Coast Guard spill prevention and response at Valdez, Prince William Sound, and major ports receiving Alaskan crude including Puget Sound, the San Francisco Bay Area, and Los Angeles/Long Beach.

Set a minimum $1,000-per-barrel civil penalty for any discharge along the pipeline, terminal, or tanker route, and made the owner of the oil jointly and strictly liable alongside the party that caused the spill.

Created a Trans-Alaska Pipeline Terminal Advisory Council of local residents, fishermen, Alaska Native organizations, and environmental and business members, with the right to full access to terminal facilities and documents as a condition of operating the pipeline.

Expanded compensable spill damages to include lost tax revenues and diminished economic activity suffered by local governments, and eased the way for Alaska Native corporations to bring oil pollution claims on lands not yet formally conveyed to them.

Established a permanent presidential task force to audit the entire pipeline system, including whether the operator was complying with its right-of-way permits, and an Alaska Oil Spill Recovery Institute to study the Exxon Valdez spill's long-term effects.

analysis.who_pays: Alyeska Pipeline Service Company and the companies that own and ship Alaskan crude, through the per-barrel fee, unlimited spill liability, and per-barrel penalties; a small share of those costs would likely have been passed to consumers at the pump.

drawbacks.text: The 5-cent-per-barrel fee and higher penalties raise costs for companies shipping Alaskan crude, some portion of which reaches consumers at the pump — though the fee works out to a tiny fraction of a cent per gallon of gasoline.

Good-faith objection: Congress put the 1973 liability limits in place to make the pipeline financeable in the first place; removing the cap and imposing open-ended, joint liability on every owner of the oil could have raised insurance costs or made some shippers reconsider participating.

The bill created three new oversight bodies — a presidential task force, an advisory council, and a research institute — funded by the fee and subject to annual appropriations, adding a permanent layer of federal and state administration.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fell on a small, well-capitalized group of pipeline and shipping companies, while the downside risk the bill guarded against was large: the bill's own findings noted the Exxon Valdez cleanup and damages could cost several billion dollars and that it was unclear whether all victims would be fully compensated under the existing capped fund. The design was reasonably careful — penalties scaled to fault, an independent audit required to avoid conflicts of interest, and explicit protection for state laws — but the fund's spending depended on annual appropriations, which could have slowed it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill died in committee: after referrals to three House committees and a single subcommittee hearing, the record shows the effort was routed into a broader oil pollution bill, H.R. 1465, and H.R. 3277 itself never received a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller introduced the bill on September 14, 1989, nearly six months after the Exxon Valdez ran aground in Prince William Sound and spilled 11 million gallons of crude oil, the largest spill in U.S. history.

The bill was referred to three House committees — Interior and Insular Affairs, Merchant Marine and Fisheries, and Public Works and Transportation — the day it was introduced, and to several subcommittees over the following weeks.
Its only hearing was a September 26, 1989 session of the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Navigation; no committee ever voted to send the bill to the floor.
On November 9, 1989, the record points to H.R. 1465, a broader oil pollution bill, as the vehicle carrying the issue forward; no further action was ever taken on H.R. 3277.
The bill never reached the House floor, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 without it coming to a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The trans-Alaska pipeline operator and the companies shipping oil through it kept the 1973 statutory liability limits and avoided the new fee, penalties, and citizen access rights for the rest of that Congress; the ideas resurfaced the next year in the broader Oil Pollution Act of 1990, passed through a different bill.

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 14, 1989, in response to the Exxon Valdez spill.

for.name: Rep. Richard Durbin

for.name: House Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Navigation
for.role: Subcommittee of Merchant Marine and Fisheries

against.name: Chairs of the House Interior, Merchant Marine, and Public Works committees
against.role: Committee chairs holding the referred bill
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill to the floor or scheduled a committee vote; the record ends with subcommittee referrals and one hearing.

against.name: Trans-Alaska pipeline operators and oil tanker companies
against.what_they_did: Faced losing their statutory liability cap and absorbing a per-barrel fee and spill penalties; the oil shipping industry campaigned against unlimited spill liability during this period.

sides.party_line_note: Only two House Democrats sponsored the bill and no vote was ever recorded in either chamber, so support and opposition never took a measurable partisan shape.

industries.industry: Oil pipeline operators (Alyeska Pipeline Service Co.)
industries.note: The bill repealed the statutory cap on the operator's pollution liability, required cooperation with a citizens' council with full access to facilities as a condition of the right-of-way, and subjected the whole system to an independent presidential audit. People in spill-prone coastal communities would have gained an operator with real financial exposure to the damage it caused.

industries.industry: Oil tanker companies and crude oil shippers
industries.note: The bill made owners of the oil jointly and strictly liable for spill penalties at a minimum of $1,000 per barrel and imposed a 5-cent-per-barrel fee; tanker failures were central to the Exxon Valdez disaster the bill responded to.

The bill's findings documented severely damaged commercial fisheries and reduced tourism after the Valdez spill; the trust fund, advisory council, and research institute were aimed at preventing and compensating the next spill that would again devastate these livelihoods.
